card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy transition-metal carbides be designed to exhibit tunable plasmonic properties in the near-IR to visible range while maintaining high thermal stability and mechanical hardness?. System: High-entropy transition-metal carbides (PHECs), specifically the archetype HfTa4C5 and a set of 14 six-element alloys (Carbon + 5 transition metals from groups 4, 5, and 6: Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W). Processing: Computational: High-throughput disorder modeling using the Partial Occupation (POCC) method within the AFLOW framework to generate Boltzmann ensembles of superlattices, followed by time-dependent density-functional perturbation theory (TD-DFPT) calculations using VASP and turboEELS. Experimental: Ball-milling of TaC and HfC powders (4:1 ratio) followed by Field Assisted Sintering Technology (FAST) at 2100–2400 °C, 40–55 MPa, and 30–40 min hold times.. Test conditions: Computational: Optical limit (q=0) and varying transferred momentum (q); temperatures up to 1500 K. Experimental: Electron-energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) on HfTa4C5 cross-sections at beam energy 300 keV, with temperatures ranging from room temperature (~25 °C) to 1200 °C.. Findings: HfTa4C5 exhibits a crossover energy (E0) at 2.41 eV (simulated) and 2.7 eV (experimental), marking a metal-to-dielectric transition in the visible range.; The plasmonic response of PHECs can be tuned from the near-IR to visible by varying the transition metal components and their concentration.; Systems 3-HfNbTaTiZrC5 and 14-HfNbTaTiWC5 show the highest effective EELS intensity (h) and lowest energy loss dissipation, indicating good plasmonic properties.; The crossover energy E0 spans a wide range from near-IR to visible, increasing monotonically with the atomic number of constituents within each group.; The screened plasmon resonance in HfTa4C5 remains clearly recognizable up to 1500 K, demonstrating stability far above the melting points of standard plasmonic metals like Ag and Au.; Substitution of Hf with 3d metals (V, Cr) leads to plasmonic resonance deterioration, while group 6 metals (W, Mo) cause broadening of the EELS peak.; The presence of Ta is necessary but not sufficient for obtaining good plasmonic PHECs; the best results come from combining high-Z elements from groups 4 and 5 (Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta).. Mechanism: The plasmonic response arises from a balance between intraband transitions (Drude-like, negative contribution to real dielectric function) and interband transitions (positive contribution). The crossover energy E0 corresponds to the energy where the real part of the dielectric function switches sign, determined by the energy difference (δ) between the Fermi level and the edge of the interband transition band (b2). Higher atomic number elements shift the Fermi level deeper into the d-band, increasing δ and causing a blue-shift in E0.. Limitations: The study does not include time evolution or de-excitation processes of plasmons, which are affected by electron-phonon scattering. Experimental characterization beyond 1500 K is noted as arduous due to equipment limitations. Some systems exhibit high dissipation where peaks cannot be associated with collective plasmon-like oscillations.. Future work: The authors propose using the discovered rules to design tailored high-entropy ceramics with optical properties optimized for specific applications, such as exploiting dissipative systems for photothermal applications or using quasi-neutral elements (Ti, W) to stabilize PHECs while altering mechanical/thermal properties.. Quote: "We chose high-entropy transition-metal carbides because of their exceptional thermal, chemical stability, and mechanical properties."

card: Paper card. Question: Can an entropy-forming-ability (EFA) descriptor based on first-principles energy distribution spectra predict the synthesizability of disordered five-metal refractory carbides as homogeneous high-entropy single phases?. System: Five-metal refractory carbides (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5, HfMoTaWZrC5, HfMoTiWZrC5, HfMoVWZrC5) derived from eight metals (Hf, Nb, Mo, Ta, Ti, V, W, Zr) and carbon. Processing: Solid-state synthesis via ball milling (2 h total, 30-min intervals with 10-min rests) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2200 °C, 100 °C/min heating rate, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 5-min dwell in vacuum/argon atmosphere. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification; Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for chemical homogeneity; Nanoindentation at 27 °C ± 0.5 °C with 50 mN load for Vickers hardness (HV) and elastic modulus (E); Williamson–Hall analysis for lattice strain. Findings: The EFA descriptor correctly predicted that MoNbTaVWC5 (EFA = 125 (eV/atom)−1), HfNbTaTiZrC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1), and HfNbTaTiVC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1) would form homogeneous single phases, while HfMoVWZrC5 (EFA = 37 (eV/atom)−1) would not.; Six of the nine synthesized compositions (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5) exhibited single rock-salt fcc phases, whereas the three lowest-EFA compositions showed multiple secondary phases.; Vickers hardness of HfNbTaTiZrC5 reached 32 GPa, which is 50% higher than the rule of mixtures (ROM) prediction, and HfTaTiWZrC5 reached 33 GPa.; The Pearson correlation between the inverse EFA (EFA−1) and lattice distortion (ε) was 0.97, and the Spearman rank correlation was 0.98, validating EFA as a synthesizability descriptor.; Lattice distortion (ε) ranged from 0.063% for MoNbTaVWC5 (most homogeneous) to 0.325% for HfMoVWZrC5 (least homogeneous).; The highest-EFA composition MoNbTaVWC5 formed a homogeneous phase despite using precursors Mo2C and W2C with different structures (orthorhombic and hexagonal) and stoichiometries compared to the rock-salt product.; Vibrational contributions to formation free energy at 2000 K ranged from ~0 meV/atom to −31 meV/atom, which are significantly smaller than the configurational entropy contributions required to overcome formation enthalpy barriers (50–150 meV/atom).; A threshold of EFA ~50 (eV/atom)−1 was identified as the point above which homogeneous disordered single phases are likely to form.. Mechanism: The authors argue that a narrow energy distribution spectrum (low standard deviation σ) implies a low energy cost to access metastable configurations, promoting configurational randomness (entropy) at finite temperatures. This entropy stabilization allows the disordered rock-salt phase to remain locked in upon cooling, even when competing ordered phases exist. Enhanced hardness is attributed to mass disorder causing impedance mismatch that scatters dislocations, increasing resistance to plastic deformation.. Limitations: The study notes that the Williamson–Hall formalism does not provide particularly accurate absolute values of lattice strain (ε), though it is effective for relative comparisons. Additionally, the vibrational contribution to entropy is an order of magnitude smaller than configurational entropy, and the study did not investigate the specific effect of carbon stoichiometry on melting points.. Future work: The authors state that an investigation of the effect of carbon stoichiometry is clearly warranted to understand how vacancies might further improve high-temperature performance, although it is outside the scope of this study.. Quote: "The descriptor correctly predicts the ease with which compositions can be experimentally synthesized as rock-salt high-entropy homogeneous phases, validating the ansatz, and in some cases, going beyond intuition."

card: Paper card. Question: How can an all-dielectric metasurface simultaneously achieve high brightness, large color gamut, narrow reflection bandwidth, and diffraction-limit resolution to meet commercial requirements for structural color?. System: Silicon (Si) nanodisks on a sapphire substrate, combined with a refractive index matching layer (dimethyl sulfoxide, DMSO, n=1.48 or PMMA). Processing: Fabrication on commercially available silicon-on-sapphire (SOS) wafers using electron-beam lithography with PMMA resist, lift-off to create a Cr mask, and reactive ion etching (RIE) in an Oxford Plasma System; optical characterization via bright-field microscopy and spectrometry. Test conditions: Bright-field optical microscopy (×50 objective, NA=0.55 for spectra; ×100 objective, NA=0.9 for resolution), white light illumination, samples tested in air and infiltrated with DMSO (n=1.48) or packaged with PMMA. Findings: The experimentally demonstrated color gamut increased from 78% of sRGB in air to 181.8% of sRGB, 135.6% of Adobe RGB, and 97.2% of Rec.2020 when infiltrated with DMSO.; The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of reflection peaks narrowed to 34–40 nm in DMSO, which is 40% narrower than in air.; Background reflection from the substrate was suppressed to approximately zero when the refractive index matching layer was applied.; High reflectance was preserved at ~74% for magnetic dipole resonance across the visible spectrum with the matching layer.; Spatial resolution reached the diffraction limit with pixel sizes as small as 2 × 2 arrays of nanodisks (center-to-center distances down to 190 nm).; The color impression remained uniform and distinguishable even when pixel sizes were reduced from 5 × 5 to 2 × 2 arrays.; The roughness of the fabricated nanostructures was measured to be smaller than 10 nm with sidewalls nearly 90° in the vertical direction.; Single-crystalline Si provided a gamut area 110% and 238% larger than poly-crystalline and amorphous Si, respectively.. Mechanism: The refractive index matching layer reduces the refractive index contrast between the sapphire substrate and the environment, suppressing background reflection. Additionally, the layer pushes the electric dipole resonance closer to the magnetic dipole resonance, creating destructive interference (Kerker condition) that narrows the reflection bandwidth (FWHM) and enhances color purity.. Limitations: The text notes that previous hybrid nanostructures suffered from incompatible fabrication technologies and deformation of top layers during etching, but states that the current single-crystalline Si approach overcomes these specific limitations; no explicit limitations of the current study are stated beyond the general need for commercialization.. Future work: The authors propose that this research routes a key step towards the commercialization of structural color in dynamic displays, optical security, and information storage.. Quote: "Consequently, the experimentally demonstrated gamut has been increased to around 181.8% of sRGB, 135.6% of Adobe RGB, and 97.2% of Rec.2020."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the role of vibrational contributions in the thermodynamic stability of high-entropy carbides, and under what conditions should they be included in stability predictions?. System: (HfNbTaTiV)C, (HfNbTaTiW)C, and (HfNbTaTiZr)C (referred to as HEC-V, HEC-W, and HEC-Zr). Processing: Computational integration of the Partial Occupation (POCC) algorithm with the AFLOW Automatic Phonon Library (APL); structures relaxed until forces were below 10−3 eV/ℓ; phonon calculations used a displacement magnitude of 0.015 ℓ in supercells with at least 180 atoms; TPOCC set to 2473 K.. Test conditions: Harmonic approximation at temperatures ranging from 0 K to synthesis temperatures; comparison against binary carbide precursors (rock-salt phases) and decomposition products; Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) used for comparison.. Findings: Vibrational contributions shift the transition temperature for HEC-W by approximately 150 K, whereas they have only a small effect on HEC-V and HEC-Zr.; Mass disorder on the cation sublattice destabilizes the high-entropy carbides (increases vibrational free energy), while force constant disorder has a stabilizing effect.; The vibrational entropy change (ΔSvib) for HEC-W is 0.22 kB/atom, which is an order of magnitude larger than the 0.04 kB/atom observed for HEC-V and HEC-Zr.; The Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) incorrectly predicts HEC-V to be more strongly stabilized by vibrations than HEC-W, failing to capture phonon anomalies present in VC.; Vibrational contributions shift the decomposition phase transition temperatures for HEC-V and HEC-W to lower temperatures by 80 K and 160 K, respectively.; The carbide sublattice distorts to accommodate different metal cations, resulting in nearest-neighbor metal-carbon distances that are closer to the average of binary carbides to maximize configurational entropy.; Vibrations alone are insufficient to stabilize HEC-V against decomposition at 2000 K, as the vibrational free energy change is smaller than the distance to the convex hull.. Mechanism: The authors argue that vibrational contributions are significant when precursors or decomposition products have different nearest-neighbor environments or symmetries compared to the high-entropy carbide. Specifically, the lower symmetry of hexagonal WC compared to the rock-salt HEC-W leads to depressed vibrational entropy in the precursor, creating a large stabilization gain upon forming the disordered phase. Conversely, when precursors and the HEC share similar atomic environments (as in HEC-V and HEC-Zr), the vibrational entropy changes are minimal.. Limitations: The study relies on the harmonic approximation, ignoring anharmonic effects which become significant at high temperatures and could stabilize structures with imaginary frequencies; the calculations use the PBE functional which may affect phonon frequencies; the ideal high-temperature configurational entropy is used, which overestimates entropic contributions at lower temperatures; and the study is limited to stoichiometric samples without accounting for vacancies or interstitial carbon.. Future work: The authors suggest that anharmonic contributions should be included to improve accuracy, that the effect of the exchange-correlation functional (e.g., SCAN vs. PBE) on transition temperatures needs investigation, and that defects such as vacancies and interstitial carbon atoms should be explored in future research on high-entropy ceramics.. Quote: "The contribution of vibrations to the stability of high-entropy ceramics is still controversial."

Paper card. Question: How to generate and validate derivative structures for (HfNbTaTi)RC high-entropy carbides to ensure converged vibrational free energy calculations.. System: (HfNbTaTi)RC where R = V, W, Zr. Processing: Created 49 ordered representative structures using the AFLOW-POCC algorithm from a rock-salt parent structure (space group: Fm-3m, #225); KPPRA value increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K converged within 1 meV/atom; APL supercells generated using standard conventional representations; relaxation and static calculations performed with exact same k-point densities.. Test conditions: Vibrational free energy convergence target of 1 meV/atom at 300 K; k-point densities required to be identical for relaxation and static calculations to avoid residual force increases.. Findings: 49 ordered representative structures were created for the (HfNbTaTi)RC system.; KPPRA values were increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K was converged within 1 meV/atom.; Using different k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations leads to an increase in residual forces by up to two orders of magnitude.; This residual force increase was observed even at KPPRA values above 20,000.; Standard conventional representations were used to generate APL supercells to achieve a more spherical shape.. Mechanism: The authors argue that maintaining exact same k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations is critical to prevent large residual forces, which can occur even at high KPPRA values if densities differ.. Quote: "producing 49 ordered representative structures."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the deformation mechanisms (TRIP vs. TWIP) in face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys be accurately predicted to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off, given the limitations of the intrinsic stacking fault energy (ISFE) criterion?. System: Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni high-entropy alloys (specifically CoxCr44-xFe26Mn10Ni8 and Co36CrxFe46-xMn10Ni8 series) and literature-reported TRIP/TWIP steels. Processing: Arc melting of high-purity elements followed by homogenization at 1200°C for 1 hour and water quenching; cold rolling with 60% thickness reduction; uniaxial compression at 20% strain with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Test conditions: Room temperature (293 K) for thermodynamic calculations; microstructure characterized via EBSD and HRTEM after deformation; hardness measured using Vickers microhardness tester (100 gram-force, 10-s dwelling time). Findings: The traditional ISFE criterion fails to predict deformation mechanisms in more than 50% of the studied cases, with an accuracy of only about 56%.; The proposed UMFE/UTFE criterion accurately predicts the deformation mechanisms (TRIP vs. TWIP) in all 7 designed HEAs and tested steels, achieving 100% accuracy.; Seven new HEAs were successfully designed and experimentally verified to exhibit either TRIP or TWIP behavior based on the UMFE < UTFE or UMFE > UTFE criteria.; Co content increases the energy barrier for stacking fault and twin formation (USFE and UTFE) but decreases ISFE, UMFE, and ME energy.; Ni content exhibits a strong effect on increasing ISFE, ESFE/TEE, UMFE, and MEE, limiting its content to promote the TRIP effect.; TRIP-dominant alloys show higher hardness compared to TWIP-dominant alloys, with hardness increasing after deformation due to high-strain hardening.; In TWIP steels, the calculated ISFE was -289.2 mJ/m², making it impossible to predict the mechanism, whereas UTFE (107.3 mJ/m²) was much smaller than UMFE (243.6 mJ/m²), correctly indicating twinning dominance.. Mechanism: The competition between martensitic transformation and twinning is governed by the energy barriers defined by the difference between unstable fault energies and ISFE (UMFE-ISFE and UTFE-ISFE). Martensitic transformation prevails when the unstable martensite fault energy (UMFE) is smaller than the unstable twin fault energy (UTFE), while deformation twinning dominates if UMFE is larger than UTFE. These unstable fault energies represent the energy barriers for the formation of martensite and twin embryos, respectively, which ISFE does not capture.. Limitations: The study did not test tensile properties, which are more appropriate to evaluate the mechanical properties of the designed HEAs. Discrepancies between CALPHAD-based thermodynamic models and DFT calculations regarding fcc stability exist and could be reduced by more advanced models considering interfacial energy.. Future work: To perform systematic mechanical property evaluation, specifically tensile testing, to select the best HEAs with potential applications and to accelerate the discovery of TRIP/TWIP in a wide spectrum of alloys using the proposed design paradigm.. Quote: "Among the studied HEAs and steels, the traditional ISFE criterion fails in more than half of the cases, while the UMFE/UTFE criterion accurately predicts the deformation mechanisms in all cases."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the bulk critical resolved shear stress (CRSS), the size effect scaling exponent, the stacking fault energy, and the magnitude of solid-solution strengthening in the equatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: Equatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (FCC structure). Processing: Arc-melting of high-purity elements in argon, cold-rolling (60% reduction), recrystallization at 1,173–1,473 K; single-crystal micropillars (1.0–8.3 μm edge length) machined via FIB at 30 kV; bulk polycrystals with grain sizes of 8, 70, and 340 μm. Test conditions: Micropillar compression at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10⁻¹ s⁻¹); bulk polycrystal compression at room temperature and 77 K (strain rate 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹); TEM analysis at 200 kV. Findings: Bulk room temperature CRSS is estimated at 33–43 MPa, approximately 10 times higher than that of pure nickel (~3.2 MPa).; CRSS follows an inverse power-law scaling with pillar size with an exponent of –0.63, independent of crystal orientation.; Stacking fault energy is determined to be 30 ± 5 mJ/m² based on Shockley partial separations of 3.5–4.5 nm (screw) and 5–8 nm (edge).; Yield stress at 77 K (260 MPa for 340 μm grain size) is slightly more than twice the yield stress at room temperature (127 MPa).; Dislocations are planar and smoothly curved with no preferred line orientation, indicating no significant anisotropy in edge and screw mobilities.; The shear-modulus-normalized CRSS of the HEA corresponds to a hypothetical binary alloy with 20–50 at.% solute concentration and ~4% atomic size misfit.; Young's and shear moduli are ~10% smaller than pure Ni, while the bulk modulus is 24% smaller than pure Ni.. Mechanism: The high CRSS is attributed to thermal solid-solution hardening driven by atomic size misfit (~4% between Cr and Co/Fe) rather than severe lattice distortion alone; the low stacking fault energy combined with a high shear modulus leads to wide partial separations that inhibit cross-slip, while the absence of orientation dependence suggests similar mobilities for edge and screw segments.. Limitations: The study notes that Goldschmidt radii may not provide accurate size misfit values, requiring ab initio calculations to estimate the true misfit of ~4.1%; the solid-solution hardening estimate is described as a rough order-of-magnitude calculation.. Future work: The authors state that full results of deformation experiments on bulk single crystals of the HEA will be published elsewhere and that additional studies are needed to improve understanding of factors like impurity contamination affecting CRSS.. Quote: "CRSS depends on pillar size with an inverse power-law scaling exponent of –0.63 independent of orientation."

W2069675613.title: Stacking faults and f.c.c. (γ) → h.c.p. (ϵ) transformation in -type stainless steel

card: Paper card. Question: How can twinning be the primary deformation mode in metastable face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys with negative or very small positive stacking fault energies, challenging existing phenomenological models?. System: Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10 (30 ≤ x ≤ 45), CrMnFeCoNi, and CrCoNi. Test conditions: Temperature range from 100 K to 500 K; affine shear strains of 0.8% and 1.2%; paramagnetic state modeled by disordered local magnetic moment approximation. Findings: For Fe80−xMnxCo10 alloys, twinning is favored over stacking faults when Mn content x ≥ 33, despite the fcc lattice being thermodynamically unstable (negative ΔF).; The metastable twinning (MTW) phenomenon occurs in CrMnFeCoNi between approximately 300 K and 460 K, where twinning is activated despite negative ΔF.; All three studied alloys exhibit γusf ≈ γutf with small or negative intrinsic stacking fault energy (γisf), a shape distinct from conventional fcc alloys.; Increasing affine shear strain increases the difference (γ¯SF - γ¯TW), thereby favoring twin nucleation; for CrMnFeCoNi, strains ≳0.7% induce MTW at all temperatures below ~460 K.; The twinning fraction (fTW) in alloys exhibiting MTW can surpass the previously established upper limit of 50%; for Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10, fTW is calculated to be 53%.; Classical SFE-based models fail to predict twinning in these systems because they require positive SFE > 10–16 mJ m−2, whereas MTW occurs with SFE values between -16.5 and 2.3 mJ m−2.; The condition for MTW is defined by δ < γisf/2 < σ*, where δ is the deviation from the universal scaling law and σ* is the pseudo-interfacial energy (approx. 4–9 mJ m−2).. Mechanism: Twinning is driven by the specific shape of the generalized stacking fault energy (γ-surface) where γusf ≈ γutf and γisf is small or negative, combined with the effect of inherent affine shear strain prior to slip. This strain increases the effective energy barrier for stacking faults relative to twinning, allowing twinning to dominate even when the fcc phase is thermodynamically unstable (ΔF ≤ 0). The phenomenon is governed by the condition δ < γisf/2 < σ*, where the chemistry and strain conditions allow the system to cross deformation mode boundaries that traditional models predict should lead to martensitic transformation.. Limitations: The study notes that while MTW is predicted for CrCoNi with increasing affine shear strain, the specific temperature range for this behavior was not fully explored in the provided text compared to the other alloys, and the analysis relies on theoretical calculations of intrinsic material parameters.. Future work: The authors propose that the disclosed behavior calls for a critical revision of previously adopted design criteria regarding twinning-induced plasticity and suggests opportunities for optimizing the mechanical response in engineering materials by tailoring metastable twinning.. Quote: "We demonstrate that twinning can be the primary deformation mode in metastable face-centered cubic alloys with a fraction that surpasses the previously established upper limit."

card: Paper card. Question: Can the stacking fault energy (SFE) be treated as a unique intrinsic property in concentrated alloys, and are dissociation distances still governed solely by SFE when the average SFE is zero or negative?. System: Model NiCo concentrated solid solution alloys (specifically Co70Ni30, Co85Ni15, and Co90Ni10 compositions). Processing: Atomistic simulations using the Kim et al. Modified Embedded Atom Method potential; dislocations created via anisotropic displacement-field solution in simulation cells of 27,213,840 atoms; thermalized at 78 K and 850 K using Nose–Hoover thermostat under NVT conditions; energy minimization via conjugate gradient algorithm; decorrelation stress calculated by incrementally increasing target shear stress (σyz) by 40 MPa.. Test conditions: Temperatures of 78 K and 850 K; zero external stress for dissociation equilibrium; shear stress applied for decorrelation force measurements; simulation box length Lx = 1100 Å; dislocation line lengths varied from 69 to 1195 Å.. Findings: Equilibrium separation distances remained finite for alloys with positive SFE (57.3 Å), zero SFE (84.9 Å), and negative SFE (109.5 Å) at 78 K, contrary to theoretical expectations for zero/negative SFE.; The average SFE values at 78 K were 19.8 mJ/m² for Co70Ni30, -0.8 mJ/m² for Co85Ni15, and -7.4 mJ/m² for Co90Ni10.; The standard deviation of local SFE values was 24.0 mJ/m² for Co70Ni30, 19.4 mJ/m² for Co85Ni15, and 17.5 mJ/m² for Co90Ni10.; The decorrelation force in zero and negative SFE alloys exceeded the upper bound of the local SFE distribution, indicating an additional resisting force.; The decorrelation force in the negative SFE alloy (Co90Ni10) was equal to the solute/dislocation interaction force (Fs), and nearly equal in the zero SFE alloy.; Direct solute–dislocation interaction energy predictions for the resisting force ranged from 17 to 30 mJ/m², whereas the reduced elastic interaction model predicted only 0.8–1.3 mJ/m².; The equilibrium separation distance in the positive SFE alloy coincided with the intersection of elastic force and the maximum SFE value, but not in the zero/negative SFE cases.. Mechanism: In concentrated alloys, the SFE is not a unique value but a distribution; furthermore, the interaction of partial dislocations with the local solute environment creates a significant resisting force (Fs) due to solute/dislocation core interactions. The equilibrium dissociation distance is determined by the balance between the elastic repulsive force and the maximum of either the upper bound of the SFE distribution or the solute interaction force, rather than just the average SFE.. Limitations: The study uses a model NiCo system which is not prone to short-range order (SRO) formation, meaning SRO contributions are not included in the force balance equation for this specific system.. Future work: The authors suggest that in real alloys with a tendency for SRO formation, the SRO contribution should be added to the force balance equation, and that other sources of resistance might be present in application to real alloys.. Quote: "We use atomistic simulations in a model NiCo alloy to study the dislocation dissociation process in a range of compositions with positive, zero, and negative average SFE and surprisingly observe a stable, finite splitting distance in all cases at low temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the synthesis methods and operating temperatures influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and tribological performance (friction and wear) of high-entropy coatings (HECs) in various industrial applications?. System: High-entropy coatings (HECs) including metallic (e.g., CuMoTaWV, FeCoCrNiMo0.2, AlCrTiV), ceramic (e.g., (AlCrNbSiTiMo)N, TiVCrZrWNx), and composite systems; base elements include Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Al, Ti, V, Mo, W, Ta, Nb, Zr, Si, Cu, Mn.. Processing: Fabrication via vapor deposition (magnetron sputtering, reactive sputtering, vacuum arc), thermal spraying (atmospheric plasma spray (APS), high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF)), and cladding (laser, plasma). Key parameters include substrate bias voltage (0 to -200 V), nitrogen flow rate (FN), substrate temperature (300 °C), annealing (300 °C), and feedstock preparation (mechanical alloying, gas atomization).. Test conditions: Tribological testing performed using ball-on-disk and pin-on-disk setups against counterfaces of Si3N4, Al2O3, and steels (SKH51, 100Cr6, GCR15). Tests conducted from room temperature (RT) up to 600 °C, varying sliding speeds, loads, and sliding distances.. Findings: The CuMoTaWV coating exhibited adaptive tribological behavior: lowest coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rate at RT due to Ta- and W-rich tribo-layers; galling wear at 200 °C; reduced wear at 400 °C due to adaptive CuO formation; and low COF but slightly higher wear at 600 °C due to excessive V-rich phase oxidation.; In (AlCrNbSiTiMo)N coatings, increasing substrate bias from 0 V to -200 V increased hardness from 28.2 GPa to 34.5 GPa and reduced wear rate to 1.2 × 10−6 mm3/N.m at -100 V, attributed to grain boundary strengthening and denser structure.; The (AlCrTiVZr)N film deposited at a nitrogen flow of 12 sccm achieved super-hardness of 41.8 GPa and a low wear rate of 2.3 × 10−7 mm3/N.m.; The FeCoCrNiMo0.2 coating fabricated via APS showed a volume wear rate of 3.9 × 10−5 mm3/N.m, significantly lower than the HVOF coating (4.8 × 10−4 mm3/N.m) and the substrate (5.4 × 10−4 mm3/N.m).; TiVCrZrWNx coatings formed a self-lubricating V2O5 phase during rolling friction, reducing the friction coefficient to 0.38.; The (CrNbSiTiZr)C film exhibited a minimum friction coefficient of 0.3 and a wear rate of 4.2 × 10−6 mm3/N.m due to the formation of a transfer film and high H/E (0.151) and H3/E2 (0.747) ratios.; Annealing the CuMoTaWV film at 300 °C improved its adhesion and wear resistance at both room temperature and 300 °C compared to the as-deposited state.. Mechanism: Tribological improvements are attributed to the formation of self-lubricating oxide layers (e.g., CuO, MoO3, V2O5) at elevated temperatures, the high hardness and nano-crystalline grain structure of the coatings, the presence of secondary phases (e.g., V-rich zones), and the balance between hardness and toughness enhanced by substrate bias or plasma nitriding. Wear mechanisms vary from adhesive wear and galling at intermediate temperatures to mild abrasive wear and oxidative wear at higher temperatures.. Limitations: The text notes that results from different wear experiments using different tools and parameters may not be directly comparable. It also highlights that there is very limited information available regarding high-entropy coatings developed by vapor deposition and cold spray methods compared to thermal spraying and cladding.. Future work: The authors state that further investigation is needed to optimize process parameters, explore more manufacturing processes (especially for HEA wires and targets), and conduct more extensive and interdisciplinary tribological investigations at high temperatures to better understand the complex wear-related phenomena.. Quote: "At RT, the lowest COF and wear rate was observed due to the formation of the Ta- and W-rich tribo layer in the wear track."

Question: How does the addition of Silver (Ag) and the variation in temperature affect the tribological properties and wear mechanisms of plasma-sprayed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-based high-entropy coatings?. System: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-Ag (HEA-Ag) and Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti (HEC) coatings formed on carbon steel. Processing: Plasma spraying. Test conditions: Temperature range from 25 to 750 °C; ball-on-disk sliding; counterface not explicitly named in the specific Li et al. summary but implied standard tribological testing. Findings: At high temperatures (600–750 °C), the HEA-Ag coating achieved a friction coefficient of 0.253 and a wear rate of 0.89 × 10−5 mm3/N.m at 750 °C.; The wear rate of both HEA and HEA + Ag coatings was significantly lower than that of tool steels SKH 51 and Q 125 at all test temperatures.; At low temperatures (RT to 400 °C), tribological properties depended on mechanical properties and Ag lubrication.; The addition of Ag had little effect on the friction coefficient at high temperatures.; The as-sprayed coatings comprised a major FCC solid solution with minor BCC phase.; A lubricious film consisting of Ag and various oxides formed on the frictional surface.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the outstanding tribological properties at high temperatures to the formation of a lubricious film on the frictional surface consisting of Ag and various oxides, which contributes to low friction and wear. At low temperatures, the properties are governed by the mechanical properties of the coating and the solid lubrication provided by Ag.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations for this specific study, only that the study investigated the effect of Ag addition and temperature.. Quote: "a relatively low friction coefficient (0.253) and wear rate (0.89 × 10−5 mm3/N.m) was achieved at 750 °C for HEA-Ag coating"

W2534691303.title: A critical review of high entropy alloys and related concepts

card: Paper card. Question: Can configurational entropy be engineered to stabilize a single-phase solid solution in a five-component oxide system where the constituent binary oxides do not form solid solutions, and can this transition be reversed?. System: Equimolar mixture of MgO, CoO, NiO, CuO, and ZnO (labeled E1). Processing: Solid-state synthesis: powders milled for 2 h, pressed into pellets at 31,000 N, fired in air at temperatures ranging from 700 to 1,100 °C with 50 °C increments, and quenched; thin films prepared via pulsed laser deposition at 600 °C with 3 J cm⁻² energy density.. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring phase evolution from 700 to 1,100 °C; differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ XRD at 5 °C min⁻¹; EXAFS at Advanced Photon Source 12-BM-B; STEM-EDS analysis at 200 kV.. Findings: Full conversion to a single-phase rocksalt structure occurs between 850 and 900 °C, with no additional peaks observed above this range.; Removing any single component from the five-component mixture results in a multiphase material when equilibrated at 875 °C for 12 h.; Deviations from equimolarity by ±2, ±6, and ±10% increase the transition temperature to single phase, confirming the entropic driving force.; The phase transformation from multiphase to single phase is endothermic, with a measured enthalpy change of approximately 12 kJ mol⁻¹ (±2 kJ mol⁻¹).; EXAFS data shows cation-to-anion first-neighbour distances are identical within ±0.01 Å for Zn, Ni, Cu, and Co, consistent with random distribution.; STEM-EDS mapping reveals chemically and structurally homogeneous material with no evidence of phase separation or clustering at the atomic scale.; A small mass loss of approximately 1.5% occurs at the transition due to the reduction of 3+ to 2+ cations during the conversion of spinel intermediates to rocksalt.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high configurational entropy of the five-component equimolar mixture overcomes the positive enthalpic penalties associated with structural transitions (specifically for CuO and ZnO) and mixing, stabilizing the single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. The entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy becomes dominant, driving the reversible transition from a multiphase state to a random solid solution where cations occupy a single sublattice homogeneously.. Limitations: The authors note that quantitative calorimetry presents challenges, and the assumption of ideal mixing for enthalpy calculations is a simplification; literature reports indicate finite and mixed-sign enthalpies of mixing that are not fully captured by the reference transition enthalpy values.. Future work: The authors propose that entropic stabilization should be explored in other systems with intermediate anions, such as chalcogenides, nitrides, and halides, particularly where covalent character is modest, and call for rigorous theoretical exploration of the crystallographic model where intermediate anions render cation sites energetically equivalent.. Quote: "entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the microstructure evolution, microhardness, and corrosion behavior of (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 high-entropy alloy coatings fabricated by plasma spraying on Q235 steel substrates?. System: (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 high-entropy alloy coating on Q235 steel substrate. Processing: Vacuum plasma spraying (ZP-2000, DWAUTO) using atomized powder; arc power 30 kW, current 500 A, Ar flow 45 L/min, powder delivery gas 4 L/min, spraying distance 100 mm. Test conditions: Microhardness tested at 500 g load for 15 s; electrochemical polarization in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 298 K, potential range −0.5 to 0.5 V, scan rate 1 mV/s. Findings: A new Laves phase formed in the coating compared to the powder, which contained only a simple FCC phase.; Elemental segregation occurred with Cr and Nb enriched in the interdendritic phase, while Co, Fe, and Ni concentrated in the dendritic region.; The transition zone width at the coating-substrate junction was merely 2 μm.; The microhardness of the coating was 321 HV0.5, significantly higher than the substrate's ~122 HV0.5.; The coating exhibited a significantly higher pitting potential and lower passivation current density than other HEA coatings in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.; Selective corrosion occurred where the interdendritic phase rich in Nb and Cr was preferentially corroded as an anode.; Tiny dish-shaped pitting pits with diameters of 1~5 μm were observed only in the gray (interdendritic) phase region.. Mechanism: The formation of the Laves phase and elemental segregation is attributed to the faster cooling rate of plasma spraying and differences in melting points (Cr: 2133 K, Nb: 2750 K vs. Co: 1770 K, Fe: 1811 K, Ni: 1728 K). The excellent corrosion resistance is due to a dense passivation film containing Cr2O3 and Nb2O5, while selective corrosion occurs because the standard potential of Nb (−1.1 V) and Cr (−0.74 V) is more negative than Fe, Ni, and Co, causing the Cr/Nb-rich interdendritic phase to act as an anode once the film is damaged.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The width of transition zone was merely 2 μm."

card: Paper card. Question: Can an Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating be successfully fabricated on an AZ91D magnesium alloy substrate via laser cladding to improve its wear and corrosion resistance, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating on AZ91D magnesium alloy substrate; mixed elemental powders of Cu, Ni, Al, Co, Cr, and Fe (99 wt % purity, 48–75 μm particle size). Processing: Laser cladding using a TR050 type CO2 high-power laser under 99.999% argon protection; mixed powders ball milled, preset with 4 vol % PVA solution (0.6 mm thickness); laser power 3000 W, scanning speed 10 mm/s, spot diameter 4 mm, overlap rate 25%. Test conditions: Dry sliding wear: 98 N load, 0.4187 m/s speed, 75 mins duration (1884 m distance), bearing steel (AISI52100) friction pair; Corrosion: potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt % NaCl solution, −2.5 V to 1.5 V range, 1 mV/s scan rate; Microhardness: 100 g load, 15 s dwell time. Findings: The coating consists of a simple FCC solid solution phase with fine dendritic microstructure.; Microhardness of the coating is HV0.1365, approximately 3.7 times higher than the AZ91D matrix (HV0.198).; The coating's wear weight loss is about 2.5 times smaller than that of the AZ91D matrix.; Wear rate of the coating is 11.93 μg/s compared to 30.38 μg/s for the AZ91D matrix.; The coating exhibits abrasive wear, whereas the AZ91D matrix exhibits adhesive wear.; Corrosion potential (Ecorr) of the coating is −0.998 V, significantly more positive than the AZ91D matrix (−1.46 V).; Corrosion current density (icorr) of the coating is 1.60 × 10−4 A/cm2, lower than the AZ91D matrix (6.20 × 10−4 A/cm2).; Copper segregates significantly in the inter-dendrite regions due to positive mixing enthalpies with other elements.. Mechanism: The high microhardness and wear resistance are attributed to solid solution strengthening and fine grain strengthening from the rapid solidification process, combined with the alloy's superior work-hardening capacity which allows the coating to shear off steel debris that then acts as abrasive particles. The improved corrosion resistance is attributed to the formation of dense chromium, aluminum, and nickel oxides on the surface, which protect against the aggressive attack that occurs on the loose, porous magnesium oxide film of the AZ91D substrate.. card: Paper card. Question: How does grain size influence the tribological behavior, wear mechanisms, and wear resistance of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloys under varying normal loads and sliding speeds?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) with fine grain (FG, ~2.9 μm) and coarse grain (CG, ~63.4 μm) microstructures. Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals followed by drop-casting into a copper mold, forging at 1000 °C, cold rolling (80% reduction), and annealing at 800 °C for 30 min (FG) or 1000 °C for 60 min (CG). Test conditions: Reciprocating sliding friction against a 10 mm Si3N4 ball under dry conditions at room temperature; normal loads of 5 N and 30 N; sliding speeds of 1, 5, and 10 mm/s; sliding time of 1200 s. Findings: The average grain size was 2.9 μm for the fine grain (FG) sample and 63.4 μm for the coarse grain (CG) sample.; The hardness of the FG sample was approximately 4.9 GPa, significantly higher than the CG sample's 3.4 GPa.; Under low load (5 N) and low speed (1 mm/s), the primary wear mechanism for both samples was adhesive wear.; With increased sliding speed, the wear mechanisms evolved to include adhesive wear and oxidation wear.; Under high load (30 N) and high speed, the wear mechanisms included adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation.; The specific wear rate of the FG sample was significantly lower than that of the CG sample across all tested conditions.; The oxide layer formed on the CG sample surface was prone to cracking and fracture, whereas the FG sample's oxide layer remained more intact.; Increasing the normal load from 5 N to 30 N resulted in a decrease in the friction coefficient due to the formation of a lubricating oxide layer.. Mechanism: The fine grain size provides higher surface strength and hardness, which improves wear resistance. Under friction heat, coarse grain samples soften more easily, causing their oxide layers to fracture and leading to increased wear. At high loads, the formation of a continuous oxide layer acts as a lubricant, reducing the friction coefficient, but the durability of this layer depends on the grain size and resulting hardness.. Quote: "The fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength."

card: Paper card. Question: How does a dual-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure in an equiatomic AlCrFeNiV high-entropy alloy influence its hardness and wear resistance under dry and lubricated sliding conditions?. System: Equiatomic AlCrFeNiV high-entropy alloy (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni, V). Processing: High-energy ball milling (SPEX 8000 mill, 2 h, ball-to-powder ratio 10:1, argon atmosphere) followed by spark plasma sintering (1100 °C for 1 h, 40 MPa axial pressure) and furnace cooling. Test conditions: Vickers hardness (5 N load, 15 s hold); reciprocating sliding wear against Al2O3 balls (10 N load, 0.18 m s−1 sliding speed, 30 min duration) under dry and lubricated (deionized water) conditions at ambient temperature. Findings: Hardness reached 1076 ± 15 HV0.5, significantly higher than previously reported values.; The microstructure consists of two BCC phases: BCC1 (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni) and BCC2 (enriched with 61.9 at.% V and Cr).; Average grain size was measured at 450 nm.; Wear rate under dry conditions was 17.2 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1.; Wear rate under lubricated conditions was 12.4 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1.; Average coefficient of friction (COF) was 0.34 in dry conditions and 0.15 under lubrication.; Hertzian contact stress at 10 N load was calculated to be 1887 MPa.; Oxygen content on the worn surface in dry friction was 2.2 at.% higher than in lubricated friction.. Mechanism: The superior hardness and wear resistance are attributed to solution strengthening from the mixture of two different BCC systems, high-density grain and phase boundaries acting as barriers to dislocation movement, and the inhibitory effect of the hard BCC2 phase on grain boundary movement and plastic flow. The wear mechanism involves abrasive wear, delamination, and oxidation, where a dense but locally unstable oxide layer forms and fractures, while the tight binding between BCC1 and BCC2 inhibits interfacial crack formation.. card: Paper card. Question: How do cold spraying (CS) and high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) spraying methods, combined with vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, 700 °C, and 900 °C, affect the microstructure, hardness, and corrosive wear properties of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings in simulated seawater drilling fluid?. System: CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings on 35CrMo steel substrate. Processing: Coatings prepared by cold spraying (CS) and high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying (HVOF) using hydrogen as fuel; followed by vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, 700 °C, and 900 °C for 2 h with a heating rate of 10 °C/min in a vacuum of <10⁻⁴ Pa. Test conditions: Friction and wear tests conducted in simulated seawater drilling fluid using a Φ6 silicon nitride ball, 10 N normal load, 5 Hz frequency, 1800 s duration, and 6 mm stroke. Findings: CoCrFeNiMn coatings prepared by CS and HVOF exhibit dense structures with porosity of approximately 1.1% and 1.4%, respectively, and bond well with the substrate.; Both CS and HVOF coatings achieve maximum microhardness after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, with values of 487.6 HV0.1 and 352.4 HV0.1, respectively.; The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹) of the HVOF-500 °C coating.; Wear rates for both coating types at room temperature are very close, at 0.2952 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹ (CS) and 0.3016 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹ (HVOF).; Heat treatment at 700 °C and 900 °C causes a decrease in microhardness and an increase in wear rates due to grain coarsening and the formation of soft phases.; The HVOF coating exhibits higher porosity and more obvious peeling compared to the CS coating due to its layered thermal spray structure.; The wear mechanisms identified include adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear, and oxidation wear, with CS being mainly abrasive and HVOF showing more oxidative and adhesive wear.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the peak hardness and lowest wear rate at 500 °C to the formation of a heterogeneous structure with nanotwins in recrystallized grains and high-density dislocations. At higher temperatures (700–900 °C), complete recrystallization leads to grain coarsening and the formation of soft FCC matrix and B2 precipitates, reducing yield stress and hardness. Oxidation wear in HVOF coatings is exacerbated by the growth, rupture, and periodic peeling of oxide layers at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the HVOF coating has higher porosity and a layered structure leading to more peeling compared to CS.. Future work: The authors do not explicitly propose future work in the provided text.. Quote: "The two types of coatings achieve maximum hardness after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C; the Vickers microhardness of CS-500 °C and HVOF-500 °C are 487.6 and 352.4 HV0.1, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Hafnium (Hf) in varying amounts (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.42) to CoCrFeNi high entropy alloys affect the microstructure, phase composition, thickness, and diffusion mechanisms during boronizing and siliciding processes?. System: CoCrFeNiHfx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.42) high entropy alloys. Processing: Vacuum arc melting (2.1 × 10–6 mbar, 700 mbar Ar, 5 re-melts) followed by powder pack boronizing/siliciding using Ekabor II™ (90% SiC, 5% B4C, 5% KBF) at 1000 °C for 5 h in an electrical box furnace. Test conditions: Surface treatment at 1000 °C for 5 h; characterization via XRD (Cu-Kα, 20–80°, 1°/min), SEM, and EDS; cross-sectional analysis of samples cut in the middle. Findings: The combined thickness of the silicon-rich layer and boride layer (SL-1 + BL) decreased from 70 µm for CoCrFeNi to 63 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.1), 20 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.2), and 15 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.42).; The thickness of the transition/diffusion zone (DZ) increased with Hf content: 60 ± 4 µm (CoCrFeNi), 50 ± 3.5 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.1), 97 ± 9 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.2), and 126 ± 6 µm (CoCrFeNiHf0.42).; XRD analysis identified the boride layer (BL) as containing Ni2Si, FeB, Fe2B, Co2B, and Cr5B3 phases.; In CoCrFeNi, Si atoms accumulated close to the BL but did not penetrate the substrate, whereas in CoCrFeNiHfx alloys, Si atoms penetrated through the Ni-rich Ni7Hf2 phase.; The microstructure transformed from single-phase FCC in CoCrFeNi to FCC + Ni7Hf2 (x=0.1) and finally to FCC + C15 Laves phases (x=0.42).; Cr-B rich precipitates (Cr5B3) were observed in the BL and DZ of CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeNiHf0.1, but in CoCrFeNiHf0.2 and CoCrFeNiHf0.42, they were detected only in the DZ.; The eutectic structure in CoCrFeNiHf0.42 has lamellae with a distance of about 0.01 µm, which accelerates B diffusion.. Mechanism: Hf addition promotes the formation of Ni-Hf rich phases (Ni7Hf2 and C15 Laves) and fine eutectic structures; these phases act as channels for Si diffusion into the substrate, while the Cr-B rich layer at the interface hinders further Si transport. The fine eutectic microstructure in Hf-containing alloys accelerates B diffusion due to short diffusion distances and dominant grain/phase boundary diffusion, leading to a thicker diffusion zone but a thinner boride layer.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "Increasing the amount of Hf in the alloys resulted in a decrease in the combined layer thickness, which was measured for CoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiHf0.1, CoCrFeNiHf0.2, and CoCrFeNiHf0.42 to be 70 µm, 63 µm, 20 µm, and 15 µm, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: How to develop a high hardness, high strength–ductility synergy, and excellent corrosion resistance of amorphous lightweight high entropy alloy film?. System: AlTiVNb high-entropy alloy (HEA) film with nominal composition AlTiVNb (1:1:1:1, at.%). Processing: High-vacuum magnetron sputtering (JCP500) onto (100) Si wafers; DC power 100 W, Ar flow 30 sccm, pressure 0.5 Pa, work distance 90 mm; film thickness 1.4 μm. Test conditions: Nano-pillar compression (height-diameter ratio 2–3, loading rate 5 nm/s); electrochemical corrosion in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature, scanning rate 1 mV/s from −0.5 V to 1.5 V. Findings: Film density calculated as 5.67 g cm−3, lower than reported similar HEAs.; Average hardness of 5.7 GPa and average modulus of 110.7 GPa.; Compressive strength of up to 3.6 GPa and deformability approaching 58% in nanopillar tests.; Current density of 4.90 × 10−8 A/cm2 and potential of −0.234 V in 3.5% NaCl solution.; Surface shows island structures with approximately several hundred nanometers width and surface fluctuation of 7.5 ± 1.8 nm.; XRD and SAED confirm an amorphous structure with no obvious lattice fringes.; No pitting pits observed on the surface after corrosion testing.. Mechanism: High strength is attributed to the disordered state, nanostructure, and lattice distortion effect from different atomic sizes; high ductility arises from ductile shear bands and the island structure which disperses deformation energy; excellent corrosion resistance is ascribed to the chemical disorder state, cocktail effect, and homogeneous amorphous structure.. Future work: This finding offers new insights into high-performance HEA films with robust mechanical and anticorrosion performances for microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials.. card: Paper card. Question: How do grain size, melting behavior, elastic properties, and deformation mechanisms change in nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys?. System: CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition). Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS software; models built via Voronoi construction with average grain sizes of 3.6, 3.0, 2.5, and 2.0 nm; equilibrated in Nose-Hoover NPT ensemble at 0 GPa and 300 K; tensile strain applied at 0.05%/ps in x-direction with NPT in y and z directions.. Test conditions: Temperature range 300–3000 K for melting; uniaxial tensile strain at 300 K with strain rates up to 5 × 10^8/s; strain levels up to 40% for stress-strain analysis.. Findings: Melting point decreases from 1940 K (single crystal) to 1430 K (3.6 nm grain size), 1340 K (2.5 nm), and is obscured by amorphization at 2.0 nm.; Shear modulus reduces by 22% and Young's modulus by 20% as grain size decreases from 3.6 nm to 2.0 nm.; Ultimate tensile strength decreases from 3.4 GPa (3.6 nm) to 3.0 GPa (2.5 nm), with the 2.0 nm sample showing a peak at 5% strain due to amorphization.; FCC composition drops from 60% (3.6 nm) to 19% (2.0 nm) at 0% strain, indicating severe amorphization at the smallest grain size.; Inverse Hall-Petch relation observed: flow stress increases with grain size (d) according to the fitted linear equation.; Plastic deformation increases with decreasing grain size for samples >2.0 nm, but decreases at 2.0 nm due to amorphization.; Diffusion coefficient of Mn is highest among all elements in the molten state at 3000 K, with an average value of 15.0 × 10⁻⁹ m²·s⁻¹.. Mechanism: At the nanoscale, plastic deformation is governed by grain-boundary mediated processes rather than dislocation motion. The primary mechanisms include grain shape change, stacking fault formation, and amorphization, which become dominant as grain size decreases to 2.0 nm, leading to a reduction in plasticity despite the general trend of increased ductility in larger nanocrystalline samples.. Limitations: The text notes deviations between theoretical and experimental values due to the complex composition of the alloy and varying experimental conditions; it also states that the amorphization at 2.0 nm makes observing volume changes during melting difficult.. Quote: "The stress-strain simulation demonstrates that the ultimate tensile strength decreases with the decrease of the grain size, while the plastic deformation increases with the decrease in grain size."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the unique compositional and microstructural features of high-entropy materials (HEMs) enhance their resistance to wear, erosion, and irradiation compared to traditional materials?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) such as CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy), AlxCoCrFeNi, NiCoFeCrMn, and NiCoFeCrPd; High-entropy ceramics (HECs) including (TaNbHfTiZr) carbides/nitrides and (Zr0.25Ta0.25Nb0.25Ti0.25)C; High-entropy composites like (Hf0.2Ta0.2Zr0.2Ti0.2Nb0.2)C doped with SiC; and HEA coatings/films such as FeNiCoAlCu, MoFeCrTiWAlNb, and CoCrBFeNiSi.. Processing: Bulk HEAs produced via powder metallurgy (mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering, hot pressing, or hot isostatic pressing) and additive manufacturing (laser metal deposition, selective laser melting, electron beam melting). HEA coatings and films synthesized via sputtering, laser cladding, resistance seam welding, or electrodeposition. HECs prepared using spark plasma sintering (SPS) or sputtering deposition for films.. Test conditions: Irradiation with 3 MeV Ni+ ions at 500 °C, 3 MeV Au+ ions, 1250 kV electron irradiation at 400 °C, 275 keV He+ ions at 400 °C, 60 keV He+ at 300 K, and 500 keV He ions. Wear tests conducted under sliding, rolling, or impact events, including scratch behavior at room temperature and elevated temperatures (e.g., above 600 °C).. Findings: HEMs exhibit higher defect formation/migration energies that inhibit defect cluster formation, making them resistant to structural damage after radiation.; Volume swelling in bulk NiCoFeCrMn is smaller than in pure nickel, with NiCoFeCrMn exhibiting 40 times higher swelling tolerance than pure nickel.; The wear rate of Al1.0CoCrFeNi is lower than Al0.3CoCrFeNi due to the formation of a hard BCC phase.; The wear rate of AlxCoCrFeNiMn dropped 63.7% at room temperature when Al content (x) increased from 0 to 1.; The surface hardness of Al0.25CoCrFeNi increased from 188 HV to 1136 HV after boronizing, reducing the wear rate by 12 times.; In NiCoFeCrMn, radiation-induced dislocation loops are smaller and denser than in binary NiFe alloy after irradiation with 3 MeV Ni+ ions at 773 K.; The average He bubble size in CrMnFeCoNi bulk HEA is smaller than pure nickel and 304 stainless steel after He-ion irradiation at 450 °C.; The friction coefficient of FeNiCoAlCu HEA coating decreased from 0.8–0.9 to ~0.3 when temperature increased above 600 °C.. Mechanism: The enhanced properties are attributed to the high-entropy effect and crystal lattice distortion, which promote higher hardness and yield stress. For irradiation resistance, compositional complexity and severe lattice distortion impede defect diffusion, causing defect clusters to migrate in a short-range 3D mode rather than the long-range 1D mode seen in pure metals, thereby suppressing void swelling. Additionally, high equilibrium vacancy concentrations in HEAs facilitate interstitial-vacancy recombination. For wear resistance, the formation of hard phases (e.g., BCC) and the 'Al-hardening' phenomenon increase hardness, while sluggish diffusion and oxide layer formation contribute to reduced wear rates.. Limitations: The configurational mixing entropy (ΔSmix) criterion fails to predict the formation of multiple solid solution phases and other intermetallic phases in some HEAs. Empirical parameters like δ and ΔHmix have overlapping areas where bulk amorphous phases, multiphase, and intermetallics form despite satisfying the criteria. The elemental differences affecting irradiation resistance remain unknown, and the effect of replacing high-activity elements like cobalt and nickel needs further study.. Future work: Future research should address the unknown elemental differences in alloy design, investigate the replacement of high-activity elements (Co, Ni) with low-activity alternatives, and acquire more data on high-temperature irradiation behavior for both bulk materials and coatings/films to accelerate the development of radiation-resistant nuclear structural materials.. Quote: "The high-entropy effect and crystal lattice distortion are attributed to higher hardness and yield stress, promoting increased wear and erosion resistance in HEMs."

Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Nb affect the wear resistance of CoNiCuFeCr HEA coatings, and what is the quantitative improvement observed?. System: CoNiCuFeCr HEA coatings with Nb addition. Processing: Deposition of HEA coatings (specific method not detailed for this specific study, but context implies coating fabrication). Test conditions: Same testing conditions as the coating without Nb. Findings: The wear resistance of the coating with added Nb is about 1.5 times that of the coating without Nb.; The study investigated the specific effect of Nb on the wear properties of the CoNiCuFeCr system.; The improvement is attributed to the reinforcement provided by the refractory element Nb.. Mechanism: The text states that refractory elements like Nb can reinforce the wear properties of HEA coatings, though it does not explicitly detail the micro-mechanism (e.g., phase formation) for this specific Nb addition beyond the general reinforcement concept.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations for this specific study, but notes generally that 'some issues still need to be addressed' regarding temperature-related serration behavior in HEMs.. Future work: The authors suggest that 'studies on serration behavior can help to reveal the underlying wear mechanism of HEMs' and that 'studies on novel self-lubricating high-entropy composites are still less explored.'. Quote: "After adding Nb, the wear resistance of the coating is about 1.5 times that of the coating without Nb under the same testing conditions."

card: Paper card. Question: Is polymorphism still possible in entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are generally believed to possess extremely high structural stability and maintain a single-phase structure?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Synthesized via gas-atomization (melt injected into high purity Ar at 4 MPa pressure); subjected to hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using a diamond anvil cell (DAC) with helium as pressure-transmitting medium; subsequently heated using resistive heating (up to 723 K) or double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating (up to ~1,400 K) at various pressures (6, 14, 26 GPa).. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to ~41 GPa; heating at ambient pressure up to 723 K; heating at 6, 14, and 26 GPa up to ~1,400 K; in situ synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring.. Findings: The fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transition starts at approximately 22 GPa and almost completes at approximately 41 GPa.; The phase transition is irreversible; the hcp phase is retained when pressure is released to ambient conditions.; The hcp phase remains stable up to 633 K at ambient pressure before transforming back to fcc.; At 26 GPa, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transition is approximately 1,400 K.; The isothermal bulk modulus (B0) is 153.9±3.0 GPa for the fcc phase and 150.2±4.6 GPa for the hcp phase.; The c/a ratio of the hcp phase remained almost constant at 1.62±0.01 during compression and decompression.; The transition is sluggish, with fcc and hcp phases coexisting over a wide pressure range of ~22 to ~41 GPa.; Decompression from different maximum pressures yields fcc/hcp composites with tunable fractions.. Mechanism: The transition occurs because the hcp structure is thermodynamically more favorable at lower temperatures and high pressures, while the fcc phase is stable at higher temperatures and lower pressures; the transition is kinetically hindered by high energy barriers and low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2), requiring high pressure to overcome these barriers to form the hcp phase.. Limitations: The transition is sluggish and irreversible, making it difficult to determine the real equilibrium phase boundary (Clapeyron coexistence curve) experimentally; grain size was not small enough for statistically reliable Rietveld refinement of volume fractions; overshooting often exists due to high energy barriers.. Future work: The authors suggest that this behavior could be general in various HEAs and propose new avenues for tailoring HEA properties via polymorphic transition-induced HEA composites, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where transition pressure could be largely decreased.. Quote: "The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: Can bulk equiatomic high-entropy carbides be synthesized from UHTC monocarbides, and what factors govern single-phase solid solution formation and mechanical property enhancement?. System: Equiatomic (Hf-Ta-Zr-Ti)C and (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high entropy Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic (UHTC) carbides; constituent monocarbides HfC, TaC, ZrC, NbC, TiC; binary (Hf-Ta)C. Processing: Ball milling of equiatomic precursor powders (200 rpm, 24 hr, WC pots, SiC media, stearic acid, 5:1 ball-to-powder ratio) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2300 °C under 16-40 MPa; optimized route included a degassing step (1800 °C, 10 min) and a 7 min dwell at 2300 °C. Test conditions: Nanoindentation testing using an Agilent/Keysight G200 Nanoindenter with a diamond Berkovich tip, Continuous Stiffness Measuring (CSM) mode, maximum penetration depth of 300 nm, strain rate of 0.05 s−1, and 64 indents per sample. Findings: The (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C composition achieved 99% density and single-phase homogeneity with the optimized processing route, whereas (Hf-Ta-Zr-Ti)C showed incomplete diffusion of ZrC.; The optimized (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high entropy carbide exhibited a hardness of 36.1 ± 1.6 GPa, significantly higher than the hardest monocarbide (HfC, 31.5 ± 1.3 GPa) and the binary (Hf-Ta)C (32.9 ± 1.8 GPa).; A relative enhancement in hardness of approximately 30% was observed compared to the rule of mixtures value (27.7 GPa) calculated from the component monocarbides.; Chemical decomposition was observed in the center of samples sintered for 10 min at 2300 °C, indicating the presence of a miscibility gap in the (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C system.; The lattice parameter mismatch of the component monocarbides was identified as a key factor for predicting single-phase solid solution formation, analogous to the Hume-Rothery atomic size misfit parameter.; The indentation modulus showed a moderate increase from ZrC through HfC~(Hf-Ta)C and TaC~NbC to the (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high entropy carbide.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the enhanced hardness arises from solid solution hardening effects caused by local non-uniformities in the lattice structure (localised strains) that impede dislocation motion, or from interesting bonding behavior leading to enhanced elastic constants; they also suggest that lattice parameter mismatch influences diffusion kinetics and solid solution formation.. Limitations: The direct comparison between measured hardness and rule of mixtures calculated hardness is not quantitatively valid without knowing the dominant room temperature slip system of the high entropy carbide; the thermal conductivity of the high entropy phase is unknown, and the mechanism for the observed miscibility gap requires further modeling.. Future work: The authors state they are undertaking ongoing future work to study the hardness behavior, specifically to test the theory regarding low thermal conductivity and to understand the miscibility behavior through further modeling studies and thermal conductivity measurements.. Quote: "revealing a significantly enhanced hardness (36.1 ± 1.6 GPa,) compared to the hardest monocarbide (HfC, 31.5 ± 1.3 GPa)"
W2805506266.title: Processing and Properties of High-Entropy Ultra-High Temperature Carbides

card: Paper card. Question: Can a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy be developed that exhibits superior radiation resistance compared to pure tungsten, specifically avoiding the formation of irradiation-induced dislocation loops under fusion-relevant conditions?. System: Quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V. Processing: Magnetron sputtering deposition from pure metal targets (99.99% purity) at room temperature and 3 mtorr pressure; deposition powers of 192 W (Cr), 312 W (V), 277 W (Ta), and 300 W (W) with 20 W bias radio frequency power; film thicknesses of ~100 nm for TEM and ~3 μm for mechanical testing. Test conditions: In situ irradiation with 1-MeV Kr+2 ions at 1073 K (dpa rates 0.0006 and 0.0016 dpa s−1) up to 8 dpa; ex situ irradiation with 3-MeV Cu+ ions at 773 K and 1050 K up to a peak dose of ~17 dpa; thermal annealing up to 1073 K; nanoindentation and nanoDMA testing. Findings: The as-deposited alloy exhibits a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of grains in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and ultrafine regions (100 to 500 nm).; A unique 4-nm lamella-like compositional layering structure was revealed by atom probe tomography (APT) in the as-deposited state.; No irradiation-created dislocation loops were observed even after 8 dpa of irradiation at 1073 K.; Black spots observed after thermal annealing and irradiation were identified as Cr- and V-rich second-phase precipitates (~3 to 5 nm in size) rather than dislocation loops.; The as-deposited samples showed a hardness of 14 GPa with near negligible irradiation hardening.; Modeling predicts the formation of Cr- and V-rich precipitates due to negative enthalpies of mixing for W-Ta, W-V, and Cr-V binaries.; Theoretical modeling suggests equal mobilities of vacancies and self-interstitials are the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the exceptional radiation tolerance arises from the equal mobilities of point defects (vacancies and self-interstitials), which maximizes the recombination probability and minimizes defect clustering. This equal mobility is attributed to the rough energy landscape induced by local lattice distortion and chemical disparity in the high-entropy alloy. Additionally, the high density of grain boundaries acts as preferential recombination/annihilation sites for defects.. Limitations: The study was conducted on thin films rather than bulk materials; the exact mechanism for the equal defect mobilities is not fully elucidated beyond the correlation with the energy landscape; the procedure to distinguish precipitates from dislocation loops using TEM breaks down for asymmetric strain fields or non-edge dislocation loops.. Future work: The authors state that the suitability of these alloys for bulk production coupled with their exceptional radiation resistance makes them ideal structural materials for applications requiring extreme irradiation conditions, implying a need for bulk synthesis and further testing.. Quote: "No sign of irradiation-created dislocation loops, even after 8 dpa, was observed."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the nature of the superconducting order parameter in high-entropy alloys, and can the observed variations in critical temperature (Tc) be explained by disorder effects?. System: (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x high-entropy alloys with nominal compositions x=0.40 and x=0.75 (actual film compositions x=0.35 and x=0.71). Processing: Magnetron sputtering on SiN wafers held at room temperature; film thickness d≈1μm; single-phase body-centered cubic (bcc) structure confirmed by X-ray diffraction and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Test conditions: High-resolution DC magnetization measurements using a Quantum Design MPMS3 VSM-SQUID magnetometer under cryogenic conditions T≥1.8 K; magnetic susceptibility χ(T) measured to determine Tc, Hc1(T), and Hc2(T); field applied parallel to film plane with 45° rotation tests. Findings: Tc values are (6.7±0.1) K for x=0.35 and (4.3±0.1) K for x=0.71 films.; Zero-temperature penetration depths are λx=0.35(0)=(896±4) nm and λx=0.71(0)=(245±2) nm.; Upper critical field zero-temperature values are Hc2,0=(81.8±0.4) kOe for x=0.35 and Hc2,0=(71.9±0.6) kOe for x=0.71.; Ginzburg–Landau coherence lengths at zero temperature are ξ0,x=0.35=(6.30±0.01) nm and ξ0,x=0.71=(6.80±0.01) nm.; Electron mean free paths are lx=0.35=(5.80±0.18) nm and lx=0.71=(5.65±0.32) nm, confirming dirty limit superconductivity.; The BCS gap parameter α is 1.74 for both compositions, consistent with weak-coupling s-wave superconductivity.; Hc1(T) is isotropic, showing no dependence on a 45° rotation of the magnetic field in the sample plane.. Mechanism: The superconducting state is described as single-band isotropic s-wave superconductivity in the dirty limit where the mean free path is shorter than the coherence length. The authors argue that because the mean free paths and mixing entropies are comparable for both compositions, the significant difference in Tc cannot be attributed to disorder effects; instead, Tc variations likely arise from changes in the density of states at the Fermi level due to electronic doping within a classical BCS framework.. Limitations: The study does not fully characterize the low-energy electronic structure at various alloy compositions to definitively explain the Tc variations beyond the density of states hypothesis.. Future work: Further theoretical and experimental studies are needed to characterize the low-energy electronic structure and its influence on Tc; testing weak coupling s-wave superconductivity in other HEA systems like those with CsCl-type lattices; exploring Tc enhancements in the two-dimensional limit near a quantum critical point.. Quote: "Despite a significant difference in the elemental composition between the x=0.35 and x=0.71 films, we find that the observed Tc variations cannot be explained by disorder effects."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the strength, ductility, and fracture toughness of an equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy compare to high-entropy alloys and conventional materials, particularly at cryogenic temperatures, and what mechanisms drive these properties?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA). Processing: Arc-melted high-purity elements (>99.9%) under argon, drop-cast into copper moulds, homogenized at 1,200 °C for 24 h, cold-forged and cross-rolled to ~10 mm thickness (60% reduction), then annealed at 800 °C for 1 h in air to achieve a recrystallized microstructure with 5–50 μm grains.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; Compact-tension (C(T)) fracture toughness tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with fatigue pre-cracking and side-grooving per ASTM E1820.. Findings: At 77 K, yield strength reached 657 MPa and ultimate tensile strength reached 1,311 MPa, representing a ~50% increase from room temperature.; Tensile ductility (failure strain) increased to ~0.9 (90%) at 77 K, a ~25% increase from room temperature.; Fracture toughness (KJIc) at crack initiation increased from 208 MPa m1/2 at 293 K to 273 MPa m1/2 at 77 K.; Crack-growth toughness at 77 K reached critical stress-intensity values of ~430 MPa m1/2 (J ~900 kJ m⁻²).; The alloy exhibited a high strain-hardening exponent (n) of 0.4 at cryogenic temperatures.; The CrCoNi alloy showed ~15% higher tensile strength, ~30% higher ductility, and ~50% higher work of fracture than the five-component CrMnFeCoNi alloy at room temperature.; At 77 K, the CrCoNi alloy displayed ~25% higher KJIc, ~27% higher ductility, and ~31% higher work of fracture compared to the CrMnFeCoNi alloy.. Mechanism: The exceptional damage tolerance results from continuous steady strain hardening that suppresses plastic instability, driven by pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Nano-twinning acts as a dominant deformation mode that provides a steady source of strain hardening, delaying necking and accommodating strain, with its intensity increasing as temperature decreases from room temperature to 77 K.. Limitations: The yield strength at 77 K was slightly lower than the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, attributed to the non-uniform grain size of the current material; the volume fraction of void-initiating inclusions was not accurately quantified relative to the five-component alloy.. Future work: Further studies are needed to accurately determine the relative volume fractions of void-initiating inclusions in the MEA and HEA and to identify their chemistry and crystal structure by TEM after extraction from the voids.. Quote: "strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2."
